screens.title: Interacting with Deployed Contracts on Testnets
screens.subtitle: From address and ABI to reading state, sending transactions, and verifying results

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how to connect a client to a contract you've already deployed to a public testnet such as Sepolia. We'll make clear what the contract address and the ABI provide, why you need a Provider for reads and a Signer for writes, and how to confirm and verify transactions once they are mined. You'll see practical steps: storing the deployed address, loading the ABI from build artifacts, instantiating a contract with Ethers. js, calling a view function to read a value, and sending a state-changing transaction that must be signed and awaited. We'll also cover how to use a public block explorer to verify the transaction hash and inspect emitted events, which is essential for debugging and user support. By the end of this chapter you'll know not only the A P I calls to make, but also the common mistakes to avoid — like trying to send a state change with a read-only provider — and a simple workflow that keeps your frontend and scripts deterministic and auditable.

keyIdea.title: Core insight
keyIdea.text: A deployed contract needs two things to interact with it: its on-chain address and its ABI. Use a Provider for free reads and a Signer when you must sign transactions to change state.

narration.text: By completing this chapter you will retrieve a deployed contract's address and ABI, use a JavaScript library to make calls to that contract, distinguish between reads and writes, and verify on-chain results through a public explorer. First, you'll learn to find and store the deployed address that your deployment script prints and to extract the ABI array from the compilation artifacts. Second, you'll instantiate a contract using a Provider for safe reads and a Signer when you need to sign transactions. Third, you'll practice calling view functions and understand why those calls do not consume gas. Fourth, you'll send state-changing transactions, await confirmations, and then use the returned transaction hash to inspect the outcome on a block explorer. Each objective focuses on practical steps and the reason why it matters, so you can avoid common mistakes like trying to mutate state with a read-only connection. These skills let you build predictable frontends and scripts that connect to testnets for safe development and debugging.

screens.title: Why address and ABI are essential
screens.subtitle: Understand the two pieces every client needs to interact with a contract

narration.text: A deployed contract on a testnet has two fundamental artifacts that let your application interact with it: the contract address and the ABI. The address is the unique identifier where the contract resides on the blockchain; it tells your client where to send calls and transactions. The ABI, short for Application Binary Interface, is a JSON array that lists each public function and event, with parameter types and return types. Think of the address as a street address and the ABI as the building's directory and rules. For example, after deployment your Hardhat script prints an address; you store that address in a configuration file or environment variable so your frontend can consistently target the same contract. The ABI is produced by the compiler and lives under artifacts/contracts/YourContract. sol/YourContract. json. A common mistake is using a mismatched ABI — perhaps from an earlier contract version — which will lead to incorrect function signatures or decoding errors. To avoid that, always extract the abi array from the artifact file that matches the deployed bytecode. Takeaway: without the address you cannot locate the contract; without the ABI you cannot form correct calls or decode events. Can you show where both artifacts live in your project now, and confirm they match the deployed build?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: Address locates the contract on-chain; ABI defines how to call it and decode events.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Why address & ABI matter
What is the Address?

The address is the contract's on-chain identifier printed by your deploy script. Store it in .env or configuration so scripts and frontends target the same contract instance consistently.

What is the ABI?

The ABI is the JSON blueprint created at compile time. It lists functions, inputs, outputs, and events. Extract the abi array from artifacts/contracts/.../YourContract.json and ship it with your client.

Example
Save COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS in .env and import the abi from the compiled artifact to instantiate your contract.
Common mistake
Using an ABI that doesn't match the deployed bytecode causes function signature or decoding errors.
Analogy
Address = street location. ABI = building directory and entry instructions.
Knowing both lets you reach the contract and speak the correct function names with the right arguments and types.
Key Takeaway

Always pair the exact deployed address with the matching ABI from your compilation artifacts before interacting.

screens.title: Locate and store deployed address and ABI
screens.subtitle: Practical steps from deployment output to frontend configuration

narration.text: After you deploy a contract with Hardhat or Truffle, the script typically prints the deployed address. The ABI is created during compilation and appears inside artifacts/contracts/YourContract. sol/YourContract. json. The practical flow is: record the address in a stable location such as a. env file, copy or import the ABI from the artifact into your frontend codebase, and version control the ABI or reference it from the build output so it cannot drift. For example, add COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS="0x..." to your. env file and require the compiled JSON to extract the abi. A common error is hardcoding an address in many places, which leads to mismatches when redeploying. Instead, use a single source of truth in configuration. Another pitfall is failing to check that the ABI corresponds to the exact solidity source you deployed. If you changed function signatures and redeployed, update the ABI before attempting calls. Takeaway: a single, versioned configuration for address and ABI reduces runtime errors and makes your client predictable and maintainable. Locate and store deployed address and ABI means record the address from deployment, extract abi from artifacts, and centralize them in configuration for consistency.. In practical terms, practical steps from deployment output to frontend configuration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Workflow
keyIdea.text: Record the address from deployment, extract ABI from artifacts, and centralize them in configuration for consistency.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Locate & Store
Step-by-step
  1. Run your deploy script and copy the printed address.
  2. Add the address to .env as COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS for scripts and frontends.
  3. Open artifacts/contracts/Counter.sol/Counter.json and extract the abi array.
  4. Import that ABI into your frontend or bundle it alongside your client code.
Pro Tip
Keep the ABI in source control or produce it as part of your build so frontend and contract remain in sync.
Common Mistake
Hardcoding addresses in multiple locations leads to confusion after redeploys. Use one canonical env entry.
Example
Add to .env: COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS="0xYourDeployedContractAddress" and in scripts read process.env.COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS so your interact script always targets the same deployed contract.
Key Takeaway

One source of truth for address and ABI prevents mismatches and simplifies deployments and client interactions.

screens.title: Provider: read-only connection
screens.subtitle: How Providers let you query blockchain state without gas

narration.text: A Provider in Ethers. js or Web3. js is a read-only interface to a node on the network. It lets your application query blockchain state — for example, call a view function like count() — without sending a transaction or consuming gas. Providers can be a JsonRpcProvider connected to a testnet RPC endpoint or a browser-injected provider for read access. When you call a view or pure function, the node executes the call locally and returns the result; no transaction is created and no block state is changed. A concrete example: if you use new ethers. JsonRpcProvider(sepoliaRpcUrl) and then instantiate the contract with that provider, calling contract. count() returns the current stored integer without cost. A common misconception is assuming a Provider can sign transactions; it cannot. Attempting to call a state-changing function with only a Provider will cause an error stating a signer is missing. Takeaway: use Providers for safe, free reads and always switch to a Signer when you intend to modify state. Provider: read-only connection means providers are read-only: ideal for view/pure calls and reading blockchain data without gas.. In practical terms, how providers let you query blockchain state without gas. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Provider role
keyIdea.text: Providers are read-only: ideal for view/pure calls and reading blockchain data without gas.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Provider
What a Provider does

A Provider connects to a node and allows read-only operations such as calling view or pure functions and querying chain data. These calls are free because they do not create transactions.

Concrete example
Using a JsonRpcProvider for Sepolia, instantiate the contract with the provider and call contract.count() to read the current value without gas.
Misconception
A Provider cannot sign transactions. Attempting to call a state-changing function with only a Provider results in an error about missing signer or private key.
Key Takeaway

Use a Provider for reads. If you need to write, attach a Signer or Wallet so the call can be signed and broadcast.

screens.title: Signer: accounts that sign transactions
screens.subtitle: Why a Signer is required for state-changing calls

narration.text: A Signer in libraries like Ethers. js represents an account capable of signing transactions and messages. Without a Signer, the network will not accept a transaction because it must be authorized by the account's private key. Examples of Signers include a Wallet constructed from a private key (used in scripts), or a browser-injected signer provided by a wallet extension such as MetaMask. When you want to call a function that modifies state — for instance increment() or transfer() — you must create a contract instance with a Signer: new ethers. Contract(address, abi, signer). A common pitfall is creating the contract with only a Provider and then attempting to call a write function, which triggers an error about a missing signer. Another important point is security: never hardcode a private key into checked-in source. Use environment variables for scripts and secure browser wallets for frontends. Takeaway: Signers are mandatory for writes and must be used carefully to protect private keys. Signer: accounts that sign transactions means signers represent accounts that can authorize and submit state-changing transactions to the network.. In practical terms, why a signer is required for state-changing calls. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Signer role
keyIdea.text: Signers represent accounts that can authorize and submit state-changing transactions to the network.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Signer
What a Signer is

A Signer holds the authority to sign and submit transactions. Use a Wallet with a private key in scripts or obtain a Signer from the browser wallet for frontends.

Security note
Do not commit private keys to source control. Use environment variables or secure browser wallets to protect keys.
Common Error
Attempting to call a state-changing function with a Provider-only contract will produce a signer missing error.
Key Takeaway

Attach a Signer to your contract instance when you need to modify chain state, and protect private keys outside of code repositories.

narration.text: Instantiating a contract in Ethers. js is simple but precise. The call new ethers. Contract(contractAddress, contractABI, signerOrProvider) creates an object with methods that map to your contract's public functions. If you pass a Provider, the methods perform read-only calls; if you pass a Signer, methods that modify state will create signed transactions. For example, if you only need to read a count variable, use a JsonRpcProvider and call contract. count() to receive the value. If you need to increment the count, create a Wallet with your private key attached to the provider and pass that wallet as the signer argument, so contract. increment() sends a transaction. A frequent misconception is that passing a signer will automatically wait for transactions to confirm — it will return a transaction response which you must await with transactionResponse. wait(). Always check whether the returned promise is a plain value (for view) or a transaction response object that requires waiting. Takeaway: choose Provider or Signer based on whether you intend to read or write, and handle transaction responses explicitly. Instantiate a contract with Ethers.js means pass a provider for reads and a signer for writes when constructing a contract instance with ethers.js.. In practical terms, new ethers.contract(address, abi, signerorprovider) explained. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Instantiation
keyIdea.text: Pass a Provider for reads and a Signer for writes when constructing a contract instance with Ethers.js.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Instantiate
Pattern
// Instantiate with a provider for reads
const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(SEPOLIA_RPC_URL);
const counter = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, provider);

// Instantiate with a signer for writes
const wallet = new ethers.Wallet(PRIVATE_KEY, provider);
const counterWithSigner = new ethers.Contract(address, abi, wallet);
Notice the contract object exposes the contract's functions. Read calls return values; write calls return a transaction response that you must await and confirm.
Example
If counter.count() returns a BigNumber, convert to string for logging. When calling counter.increment(), capture the returned tx and await tx.wait() to ensure it was mined.
Key Takeaway

The signerOrProvider argument determines whether functions perform free reads or signed writes; handle transaction responses explicitly.

screens.title: View functions vs State-changing functions
screens.subtitle: When calls are free and when they require a signed transaction

narration.text: Calls to smart contracts fall into two categories: view (or pure) functions and state-changing functions. View functions read state and are declared with view or pure in Solidity. They are executed locally by the node and do not create transactions or consume gas. For instance, reading a stored count is a view operation and is free. State-changing functions, such as increment or transfer, modify contract state and therefore must be sent as transactions, signed by a wallet; these consume gas. A common confusion is believing that calling a state-changing method on a contract instance with a Provider will work — it will not, because the call lacks a signer to authorize the transaction. Another misunderstanding is assuming tx. wait() is automatic; it is not. When you call a state-changing function you receive a transaction response, and you should await transactionResponse. wait() to confirm the transaction was mined. Example: call count() with a Provider for immediate read; call increment() with a Signer, await the tx, then call count() again to observe the change. Takeaway: know the function type before deciding whether you need a signer and gas.

keyIdea.title: Comparison
keyIdea.text: View functions are free, state-changing functions require signing and gas; choose Provider or Signer accordingly.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › View vs State-changing
View / Pure
  • Read-only calls that don't alter state.
  • Executed locally by a node, cost no gas.
  • Use a Provider to call these functions.
Concrete example
contract.count() returns a numeric value without creating a transaction.
State-changing
  • Modify contract state and create transactions.
  • Require a Signer to sign and send, consume gas.
  • Return a transaction response that needs tx.wait().
Common mistake
Calling a state-changing function with a Provider-only contract raises a signer missing error.
Check your understanding
If balanceOf is a view function and you call it via a contract instantiated with a Provider, will it cost gas? Explain your answer and why a Signer is not necessary here.

screens.title: Send transactions and wait for confirmations
screens.subtitle: Use tx.wait() to confirm inclusion and inspect gas and events

narration.text: When you send a state-changing transaction through a contract method, Ethers. js returns a transaction response immediately. That response contains a transaction hash you can share or paste into a public explorer to inspect the transaction. However, the transaction may not yet be mined. To ensure the change became part of the blockchain state, call transactionResponse. wait() and await the returned receipt. The receipt includes block number, gas used, and logs for any emitted events. A concrete flow: call const tx = await contract. increment(); then await tx. wait(); then log tx. hash and the confirmed state. A common misconception is treating the transaction response as confirmation — it is only a promise that the transaction was submitted. Another common problem is not handling failures: failures can occur during execution, so inspect the receipt status and revert reasons if available. Takeaway: always await confirmation before assuming state has changed, and use the transaction hash to inspect details on a block explorer for debugging and transparency. Send transactions and wait for confirmations means a transaction response is not a confirmation. use tx.wait() and inspect the receipt and transaction hash to verify success.. In practical terms, use tx.wait() to confirm inclusion and inspect gas and events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Confirmation
keyIdea.text: A transaction response is not a confirmation. Use tx.wait() and inspect the receipt and transaction hash to verify success.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Send & Confirm
Transaction flow
  1. Call a state-changing function with a Signer: const tx = await contract.increment();
  2. Get an immediate transaction response that includes tx.hash.
  3. Await confirmation: await tx.wait() to receive the receipt.
  4. Inspect receipt.status, gasUsed, and logs for events.
Why wait?
Waiting ensures the transaction was included in a block and that state changes are final for your application logic.
Example
After await tx.wait(), copy tx.hash into a public explorer to see confirmations, gas used, and any events your contract emitted.
Common mistake

Treating the immediate tx response as success without awaiting confirmation leads to race conditions and wrong UI state.

screens.title: Use a public block explorer to verify interactions
screens.subtitle: Why transaction hashes and explorers matter for debugging and trust

narration.text: Public block explorers provide transparency and a convenient debugging interface. After you send a state-changing transaction and obtain its hash, paste it into a block explorer for the testnet to inspect inclusion, gas usage, and events. For Sepolia this means using the network's explorer to view the transaction status and logs emitted by your contract. This is important for support: if a user reports a failed action, you can request the transaction hash and immediately diagnose whether it was mined, whether it reverted, and which events fired. Inspecting events helps confirm that state changes you expected actually occurred and reveals details about gas consumption. A common misconception is that explorers can always show revert reasons; some revert reasons require extra tooling or node support. Still, explorers are the primary way to verify on-chain activity. Takeaway: keep transaction hashes and use the explorer as a first step for transparent debugging and user assurance. Use a public block explorer to verify interactions means use a testnet explorer to inspect tx.hash for confirmation, gas usage, and emitted events to debug and validate interactions.. In practical terms, why transaction hashes and explorers matter for debugging and trust. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Explorer verification
keyIdea.text: Use a testnet explorer to inspect tx.hash for confirmation, gas usage, and emitted events to debug and validate interactions.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Verify on Explorer
What to check
  • Transaction status and number of confirmations.
  • Gas used and gas price information.
  • Logs and events emitted by your contract.
If a transaction reverted, the explorer may display the failure. Use the hash to share details with users or teammates for quick diagnosis.
Practical example
Copy the printed hash from your interaction script and paste it into the testnet explorer to confirm the increment or transfer took place and to view any emitted events.
Key Takeaway

Explorers make transactions transparent and are the first stop for debugging and user support.

screens.title: Common mistakes and how to avoid them
screens.subtitle: Signer vs Provider errors, ABI mismatches, and insecure key handling

narration.text: When interacting with deployed contracts, a small set of recurring errors causes most failures. First, invoking state-changing methods with a Provider-only contract raises a signer missing error. The fix is to pass a Signer or Wallet as the third argument when constructing the contract. Second, ABI mismatches occur when you use an ABI that does not correspond to the deployed bytecode; this leads to decoding failures or calls that do not exist. Always extract the abi from the artifact that matches the deployed contract. Third, insecure handling of private keys — such as committing them to source — poses security risks. Use environment variables for scripts and browser wallets or secure key management in frontends. Lastly, assuming a transaction is final when you receive the response rather than awaiting confirmation causes race conditions. Always call tx. wait() and inspect the receipt. Takeaway: check signer presence, verify ABI match, secure private keys, and await confirmations to avoid common runtime issues. Common mistakes and how to avoid them means ensure signer is present for writes, abi matches the deployed contract, private keys are secured, and confirmations are awaited.. In practical terms, signer vs provider errors, abi mismatches, and insecure key handling. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Avoid errors
keyIdea.text: Ensure signer is present for writes, ABI matches the deployed contract, private keys are secured, and confirmations are awaited.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Common Mistakes
Signer vs Provider
Mistake: calling a write with a Provider-only instance. Fix: instantiate contract with a Wallet or get a signer from the provider.
ABI mismatch
Mistake: using an outdated ABI. Fix: extract abi from the exact artifact produced by the current compilation.
Security & Confirmations
Mistake: committing private keys to code or not awaiting tx.wait(). Fix: use .env variables, secure wallets, and await transaction receipts before assuming success.
Check
When you see an error, first confirm signer presence, verify the ABI source, and look up the transaction hash on the explorer to understand what happened.

screens.title: Full interact.js walkthrough
screens.subtitle: A working Ethers.js script that reads count, increments, waits, and verifies

narration.text: Let's step through a complete interaction script used to talk to a Counter contract. The script reads an address from environment variables, connects to Sepolia using a JsonRpcProvider, constructs a Wallet signer with the private key, loads the artifact to extract the ABI, and then creates a contract instance with the signer. It first calls the view method to read the current count, then calls increment(), awaits the transaction confirmation with tx. wait(), logs the transaction hash for explorer verification, and finally reads the updated count. As an example, place COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS and PRIVATE_KEY in your. env and run the script with node. A misconception to watch for is printing the transaction response instead of awaiting the receipt — the printed response does not prove the transaction was mined. The key steps are: build provider, build signer, load abi, instantiate, call view, call write, await wait(), and verify the hash on the explorer. Takeaway: this flow is a repeatable pattern for safe interaction with deployed contracts on testnets. Full interact.js walkthrough means read env config, create provider and signer, load abi, instantiate contract, call read, send write, await tx.wait(), and verify the hash.. In practical terms, a working ethers.js script that reads count, increments, waits, and verifies. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Script pattern
keyIdea.text: Read env config, create provider and signer, load ABI, instantiate contract, call read, send write, await tx.wait(), and verify the hash.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › interact.js Walkthrough
Script preview
// scripts/interact.js
require("dotenv").config();
const { ethers } = require("hardhat");

async function main() {
  const contractAddress = process.env.COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS;
  const privateKey = process.env.PRIVATE_KEY;

  const provider = new ethers.JsonRpcProvider(process.env.SEPOLIA_RPC_URL);
  const signer = new ethers.Wallet(privateKey, provider);

  const CounterArtifact = require("../artifacts/contracts/Counter.sol/Counter.json");
  const counterABI = CounterArtifact.abi;

  const counterContract = new ethers.Contract(contractAddress, counterABI, signer);

  let currentCount = await counterContract.count();
  console.log("Current count:", currentCount.toString());

  const tx = await counterContract.increment();
  await tx.wait();
  console.log("Increment tx:", tx.hash);
}

main().catch(console.error);
Running the script
Set COUNTER_CONTRACT_ADDRESS and PRIVATE_KEY in .env, then run node scripts/interact.js. Watch the terminal output for the current count, transaction hash, and updated count after confirmation.
Key Takeaway

This interact script demonstrates the complete read-write-confirm cycle and the use of the transaction hash for verification.

screens.title: Configuration and security best practices
screens.subtitle: How to manage addresses, ABIs, and private keys safely

narration.text: A robust interaction workflow includes safe configuration and attention to security. Store your deployed contract addresses in a single configuration file or environment variables so the same address is used by scripts and the frontend. Keep the ABI alongside your build artifacts and version it when appropriate to ensure the contract interface remains synchronized with deployed code. For private keys used in scripts, read them from environment variables and never commit them to source control. For frontends, prefer user-driven signers such as browser wallets so the user manages keys. Another pattern is to restrict privileged operations in contracts so private keys do not grant unlimited access if leaked. A misconception is thinking a quick local script with a hardcoded key is harmless; even testnet keys can be lost and create debugging confusion. Finally, log transaction hashes and receipts for each state change so you have an audit trail for support. Module 7 › Chapter 7.2 › Configuration & Security
Centralize configuration
Use a single .env entry or config file for the deployed address and import the ABI from build artifacts. This prevents mismatches and drift across environments.
Developer tip
Add a deployment step that writes the deployed address to a known config file used by scripts and the frontend.
Protect keys and logs
Never commit private keys. Use environment variables for scripts and browser wallets for user actions. Log tx.hash and receipts for auditing and support.
Key Takeaway

Good configuration and key hygiene reduce errors and make debugging transparent and secure.

narration.text: Keep four simple concepts in mind when interacting with deployed contracts: the contract address locates the contract on-chain, and the ABI tells your client how to call its functions. Use a Provider to perform read-only calls to view functions without gas, and attach a Signer when you need to send state-changing transactions. After sending a transaction, wait for confirmation with tx. wait() and use the returned transaction hash to inspect the result on a public explorer for verification and debugging. Contract Address

ABI
A JSON blueprint describing functions and events so your client can encode and decode calls.
Provider vs Signer
Provider for reads, Signer for writes. Choose the right one to avoid missing-signer errors.
Summary Takeaway
Pair the correct address and ABI, use a Provider for free reads, attach a Signer for state changes, await confirmations with tx.wait(), and verify with a transaction hash on a public explorer to maintain transparency and reliability.

narration.text: Before running your interact scripts or wiring a frontend, keep these three reminders in mind. First, ensure the ABI you use matches the deployed contract bytecode; mismatches lead to call or decoding failures. Second, identify whether each function you call is a view or state-changing function so you know whether to use a Provider or a Signer. Third, after sending a transaction, await confirmation and use the transaction hash to inspect the result on the block explorer. These reminders help you avoid the most common issues when moving from deployment to practical DApp interactions on testnets.
